speaker: student
context: The Upanishad opens with a student's question: what power drives the mind, breath, speech and senses?
devanagari:
ॐ केनेषितं पतति प्रेषितं मनः
केन प्राणः प्रथमः प्रैति युक्तः ।
केनेषितां वाचमिमां वदन्ति
चक्षुः श्रोत्रं क उ देवो युनक्ति ॥
iast:
oṃ keneṣitaṃ patati preṣitaṃ manaḥ
kena prāṇaḥ prathamaḥ praiti yuktaḥ |
keneṣitāṃ vācamimāṃ vadanti
cakṣuḥ śrotraṃ ka u devo yunakti ||
english: Om. Willed by whom, sent by whom, does the mind fly out? Yoked by whom does the first breath go forth? Willed by whom do people speak this speech? What god yokes the eye and the ear?

school_notes.note: The question comes from someone who has turned away from the impermanent body and its works and seeks what is unchanging. They are unsure whether the body-mind complex directs the mind and senses, or something apart from it directs them by mere will.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher answers: what drives the senses is the ear of the ear and the mind of the mind, and the wise who know it become immortal.
devanagari:
श्रोत्रस्य श्रोत्रं मनसो मनो यद्वाचो ह वाचं
स उ प्राणस्य प्राणः चक्षुषश्चक्षुः ।
अतिमुच्य धीराः प्रेत्यास्माल्लोकादमृता भवन्ति ॥
iast:
śrotrasya śrotraṃ manaso mano yadvāco ha vācaṃ
sa u prāṇasya prāṇaḥ cakṣuṣaścakṣuḥ |
atimucya dhīrāḥ pretyāsmāllokādamṛtā bhavanti ||
english: It is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, the speech of speech; it is the breath of breath and the eye of the eye. Letting go, the wise, departing from this world, become immortal.

school_notes.note: The answer fits because the director of the senses is known only as the one for whose sake they work together, as a house serves someone who lives in it. The ear can reveal sound only because the ever-present light of consciousness, the Self, is there; 'letting go' means giving up identification with the senses, and 'departing' means leaving the body.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher says that the eye, speech and mind cannot reach this reality, so it cannot be taught like an object.
devanagari:
न तत्र चक्षुर्गच्छति न वाग्गच्छति नो मनः ।
न विद्मो न विजानीमो यथैतदनुशिष्यात् ॥
iast:
na tatra cakṣurgacchati na vāggacchati no manaḥ |
na vidmo na vijānīmo yathaitadanuśiṣyāt ||
english: There the eye does not go, nor speech, nor the mind. We do not know, we do not understand, how one could teach it.

school_notes.note: Eye, speech and mind cannot reach Brahman because it is their own Self, as fire burns and lights other things but not itself. Having no class, quality or action, it cannot be taught as objects are, which shows how much effort teaching and grasping it require; yet scripture can convey it, as the next words do.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher adds the traditional teaching: this reality is other than everything known and beyond the unknown.
devanagari:
अन्यदेव तद्विदितादथो अविदितादधि ।
इति शुश्रुम पूर्वेषां ये नस्तद्व्याचचक्षिरे ॥
iast:
anyadeva tadviditādatho aviditādadhi |
iti śuśruma pūrveṣāṃ ye nastadvyācacakṣire ||
english: It is other than the known, and beyond the unknown. So we have heard from those of old who explained it to us.

school_notes.note: Being other than the known, Brahman is not something to be rejected; being beyond the unknown, it is not something to be acquired. So it is one's own Self. This is learned only through the line of teachers, not by reasoning, learning or rituals.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher begins a refrain (1.5-1.9): Brahman is what makes speech, mind and senses work, not what people worship as an object.
devanagari:
यद्वाचाऽनभ्युदितं येन वागभ्युद्यते ।
तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
iast:
yadvācā'nabhyuditaṃ yena vāgabhyudyate |
tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
english: What speech cannot express, but by which speech is expressed: know that alone as Brahman, not this which people worship here.

school_notes.note: Brahman is the light of consciousness by which speech is lit and used. Set aside every description that comes from limiting conditions and know the unconditioned Self alone as Brahman, not what people meditate on as something other than the Self, such as a God separate from them.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher continues the refrain: Brahman is not something the mind can think, but what lets the mind think.
devanagari:
यन्मनसा न मनुते येनाहुर्मनो मतम् ।
तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
iast:
yanmanasā na manute yenāhurmano matam |
tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
english: What one cannot think with the mind, but by which, they say, the mind is thought: know that alone as Brahman, not this which people worship here.

school_notes.note: The mind, which includes desire, resolve, doubt and faith, cannot think the light of consciousness that illumines it. Knowers of Brahman say the mind with all its activity is pervaded by that light; know that inner Self as Brahman.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher continues the refrain: Brahman is not seen by the eye, but is what lets the eye see.
devanagari:
यच्चक्षुषा न पश्यति येन चक्षूँषि पश्यति ।
तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
iast:
yaccakṣuṣā na paśyati yena cakṣūm̐ṣi paśyati |
tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
english: What one cannot see with the eye, but by which the eyes are seen: know that alone as Brahman, not this which people worship here.

school_notes.note: People do not make it an object with the eye; it is the light of consciousness by which the eye's activity is itself known.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher continues the refrain: Brahman is not heard by the ear, but is what lets the ear hear.
devanagari:
यच्छ्रोत्रेण न शृणोति येन श्रोत्रमिदं श्रुतम् ।
तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
iast:
yacchrotreṇa na śṛṇoti yena śrotramidaṃ śrutam |
tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
english: What one cannot hear with the ear, but by which this ear is heard: know that alone as Brahman, not this which people worship here.

school_notes.note: People do not grasp it with the ear; it is the light of consciousness by which the ear itself, familiar to all, becomes known.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher ends the refrain: Brahman is not reached by the breath, but is what moves the breath.
devanagari:
यत्प्राणेन न प्राणिति येन प्राणः प्रणीयते ।
तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
iast:
yatprāṇena na prāṇiti yena prāṇaḥ praṇīyate |
tadeva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate ||
english: What one does not breathe with the breath, but by which the breath is led forth: know that alone as Brahman, not this which people worship here.

school_notes.note: 'Breath' here is the sense of smell; Brahman is not smelled like a scent, but is the light of consciousness by which smell reaches its objects.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher warns against thinking Brahman is fully known; in the last words, after reflecting, the student replies.
devanagari:
यदि मन्यसे सुवेदेति दहरमेवापि
नूनं त्वं वेत्थ ब्रह्मणो रूपम् ।
यदस्य त्वं यदस्य देवेष्वथ नु
मीमाँस्येमेव ते मन्ये विदितम् ॥
iast:
yadi manyase suvedeti daharamevāpi
nūnaṃ tvaṃ vettha brahmaṇo rūpam |
yadasya tvaṃ yadasya deveṣvatha nu
mīmām̐syemeva te manye viditam ||
english: If you think, 'I know it well,' then surely you know only a little of Brahman's form: the form that is in you, and the form that is among the gods. So I think you must still inquire into it. 'I think I know it.'

school_notes.note: The teacher unsettles the student so they will not cling to 'I know Brahman well'. Whatever is known of Brahman through limiting conditions, in the body or among the gods, is small; the infinite Brahman free of all conditions is not easily known. The student then sat alone, reflected on the teaching, tested it by reason and experience, and returned to say, 'I think I now know Brahman.'

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: student
context: The student explains with a paradox: Brahman is neither simply known nor simply unknown.
devanagari:
नाहं मन्ये सुवेदेति नो न वेदेति वेद च ।
यो नस्तद्वेद तद्वेद नो न वेदेति वेद च ॥
iast:
nāhaṃ manye suvedeti no na vedeti veda ca |
yo nastadveda tadveda no na vedeti veda ca ||
english: I do not think I know it well; yet it is not that I do not know it, and I do know it. Whoever among us understands 'it is not that I do not know it, and I do know it' knows it.

school_notes.note: Though the teacher tried to shake them, the student did not waver, relying on the teaching 'other than the known and beyond the unknown', on reasoning and on experience. Brahman cannot be known as an object, yet is not unknown, so the student declares with confidence that whoever grasps this paradox knows it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Upanishad
context: Leaving the dialogue, the Upanishad states the point in its own voice: those who claim to know Brahman do not.
devanagari:
यस्यामतं तस्य मतं मतं यस्य न वेद सः ।
अविज्ञातं विजानतां विज्ञातमविजानताम् ॥
iast:
yasyāmataṃ tasya mataṃ mataṃ yasya na veda saḥ |
avijñātaṃ vijānatāṃ vijñātamavijānatām ||
english: One for whom it is unthought has thought it; one for whom it is thought does not know it. It is unknown to those who know it, and known to those who do not.

school_notes.note: One who holds that Brahman is not an object of knowledge truly knows it; one convinced 'I have known Brahman' does not. 'Those who do not know' are people who take the senses, mind or intellect for the Self, not the wholly untaught, who would not claim to know Brahman at all.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Upanishad
context: The Upanishad says Brahman is rightly known as the awareness present in every act of knowing, and this knowledge brings immortality.
devanagari:
प्रतिबोधविदितं मतममृतत्वं हि विन्दते ।
आत्मना विन्दते वीर्यं विद्यया विन्दतेऽमृतम् ॥
iast:
pratibodhaviditaṃ matamamṛtatvaṃ hi vindate |
ātmanā vindate vīryaṃ vidyayā vindate'mṛtam ||
english: It is known when it is known in every act of awareness, for by this one gains immortality. Through the Self one gains strength; through knowledge, immortality.

school_notes.note: The Self is the witness of every cognition and is known as present in each; so known, Brahman is rightly known as eternal, pure and one. He rejects reading the Self as the agent of knowing, which would make it changing. The strength gained from wealth, allies, spells or medicine cannot overcome death; only the strength of self-knowledge, gained through the Self alone, can.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Upanishad
context: The Upanishad urges knowing Brahman in this life, since failing to do so is a great loss.
devanagari:
इह चेदवेदीदथ सत्यमस्ति
न चेदिहावेदीन्महती विनष्टिः ।
भूतेषु भूतेषु विचित्य धीराः
प्रेत्यास्माल्लोकादमृता भवन्ति ॥
iast:
iha cedavedīdatha satyamasti
na cedihāvedīnmahatī vinaṣṭiḥ |
bhūteṣu bhūteṣu vicitya dhīrāḥ
pretyāsmāllokādamṛtā bhavanti ||
english: If one knows it here, then there is truth; if one does not know it here, great is the loss. Discerning it in every being, the wise, departing from this world, become immortal.

school_notes.note: If a capable person knows the Self here, in this human birth, this life has truth and meaning; if not, the loss is the endless round of birth, ageing and death. The wise, seeing one Self in all beings, moving and unmoving, turn away from the world of 'I' and 'mine' and become Brahman.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: The Upanishad begins a parable: the gods take credit for a victory that was really Brahman's (3.1-4.3).
devanagari:
ब्रह्म ह देवेभ्यो विजिग्ये तस्य ह ब्रह्मणो
विजये देवा अमहीयन्त ॥
iast:
brahma ha devebhyo vijigye tasya ha brahmaṇo
vijaye devā amahīyanta ||
english: Brahman, it is told, won a victory for the gods, and in Brahman's victory the gods grew great.

school_notes.note: Brahman defeated the demons, enemies of the world, for the gods' sake and gave them the fruit of victory; Agni and the other gods gained glory, not knowing it was the work of the all-knowing Lord within them.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, the gods claim the victory as their own, and Brahman appears before them as a mysterious being.
devanagari:
त ऐक्षन्तास्माकमेवायं विजयोऽस्माकमेवायं महिमेति ।
तद्धैषां विजज्ञौ तेभ्यो ह प्रादुर्बभूव तन्न व्यजानत
किमिदं यक्षमिति ॥
iast:
ta aikṣantāsmākamevāyaṃ vijayo'smākamevāyaṃ mahimeti |
taddhaiṣāṃ vijajñau tebhyo ha prādurbabhūva tanna vyajānata
kimidaṃ yakṣamiti ||
english: They thought, 'This victory is ours alone; this greatness is ours alone.' Brahman knew this of them and appeared before them. They did not know what it was: 'What is this wondrous being?'

school_notes.note: The gods' pride was false. Brahman saw it and, out of compassion, so that pride would not ruin the gods as it had the demons, appeared in a wondrous form; they did not recognise it, 'yakṣa' meaning a great being worthy of worship.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, the gods send Agni, the fire-god, to find out what the mysterious being is.
devanagari:
तेऽग्निमब्रुवन् जातवेद एतद्विजानीहि
किमिदं यक्षमिति तथेति ॥
iast:
te'gnimabruvan jātaveda etadvijānīhi
kimidaṃ yakṣamiti tatheti ||
english: They said to Agni, 'Jatavedas, find out what this wondrous being is.' 'Very well,' he said.

school_notes.note: Not knowing it and afraid, the gods asked Agni, their leader and almost all-knowing, to find out.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, Agni approaches the being and boasts of his names.
devanagari:
तदभ्यद्रवत्तमभ्यवदत्कोऽसीत्यग्निर्वा
अहमस्मीत्यब्रवीज्जातवेदा वा अहमस्मीति ॥
iast:
tadabhyadravattamabhyavadatko'sītyagnirvā
ahamasmītyabravījjātavedā vā ahamasmīti ||
english: He ran towards it. It asked him, 'Who are you?' 'I am Agni,' he said, 'I am Jatavedas.'

school_notes.note: Agni fell silent near it from timidity, so it spoke first; he praised himself by giving both his famous names.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, Agni claims he can burn everything on earth.
devanagari:
तस्मिँस्त्वयि किं वीर्यमित्यपीदँ सर्वं
दहेयं यदिदं पृथिव्यामिति ॥
iast:
tasmim̐stvayi kiṃ vīryamityapīdam̐ sarvaṃ
daheyaṃ yadidaṃ pṛthivyāmiti ||
english: 'What power is there in you?' 'I could burn all this, whatever is on earth.'

school_notes.note: Asked his power, Agni says he could burn everything; 'on earth' stands for everywhere, since fire burns what is in the sky too.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, Agni cannot burn a single blade of grass and returns humbled.
devanagari:
तस्मै तृणं निदधावेतद्दहेति ।
तदुपप्रेयाय सर्वजवेन तन्न शशाक दग्धुं स तत एव
निववृते नैतदशकं विज्ञातुं यदेतद्यक्षमिति ॥
iast:
tasmai tṛṇaṃ nidadhāvetaddaheti |
tadupapreyāya sarvajavena tanna śaśāka dagdhuṃ sa tata eva
nivavṛte naitadaśakaṃ vijñātuṃ yadetadyakṣamiti ||
english: It set a blade of grass before him: 'Burn this.' He went at it with all his speed but could not burn it. He turned back from there: 'I could not find out what this wondrous being is.'

school_notes.note: Brahman in effect said: 'Burn this straw before me; if you cannot, give up your pride in being the burner of everything.' Unable to burn it, Agni turned back ashamed, his boast broken.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, the gods next send Vayu, the wind-god (3.7-3.10).
devanagari:
अथ वायुमब्रुवन्वायवेतद्विजानीहि
किमेतद्यक्षमिति तथेति ॥
iast:
atha vāyumabruvanvāyavetadvijānīhi
kimetadyakṣamiti tatheti ||
english: Then they said to Vayu, 'Vayu, find out what this wondrous being is.' 'Very well,' he said.

school_notes.note: These verses mean the same as those about Agni; Vāyu is so called from blowing or carrying scents, and Mātariśvan from moving in the sky.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, Vayu approaches the being and boasts of his names.
devanagari:
तदभ्यद्रवत्तमभ्यवदत्कोऽसीति वायुर्वा
अहमस्मीत्यब्रवीन्मातरिश्वा वा अहमस्मीति ॥
iast:
tadabhyadravattamabhyavadatko'sīti vāyurvā
ahamasmītyabravīnmātariśvā vā ahamasmīti ||
english: He ran towards it. It asked him, 'Who are you?' 'I am Vayu,' he said, 'I am Matarishvan.'

school_notes.note: These verses mean the same as those about Agni; Mātariśvan means the one who moves in the sky.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, Vayu claims he can carry off everything on earth.
devanagari:
तस्मिँस्त्वयि किं वीर्यमित्यपीदँ
सर्वमाददीय यदिदं पृथिव्यामिति ॥
iast:
tasmim̐stvayi kiṃ vīryamityapīdam̐
sarvamādadīya yadidaṃ pṛthivyāmiti ||
english: 'What power is there in you?' 'I could carry off all this, whatever is on earth.'

school_notes.note: Vāyu's claim to seize everything on earth parallels Agni's claim, with the same meaning.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, Vayu cannot move a blade of grass and returns humbled.
devanagari:
तस्मै तृणं निदधावेतदादत्स्वेति
तदुपप्रेयाय सर्वजवेन तन्न शशाकादतुम् ।
स तत एव निववृते नैतदशकं विज्ञातुं यदेतद्यक्षमिति ॥
iast:
tasmai tṛṇaṃ nidadhāvetadādatsveti
tadupapreyāya sarvajavena tanna śaśākādatum |
sa tata eva nivavṛte naitadaśakaṃ vijñātuṃ yadetadyakṣamiti ||
english: It set a blade of grass before him: 'Carry this off.' He went at it with all his speed but could not move it. He turned back from there: 'I could not find out what this wondrous being is.'

school_notes.note: The story of Vāyu repeats that of Agni with the same meaning: the boast fails before a single blade of grass.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, the gods send Indra, their king, and the being vanishes as he approaches.
devanagari:
अथेन्द्रमब्रुवन्मघवन्नेतद्विजानीहि किमेतद्यक्षमिति तथेति
तदभ्यद्रवत्तस्मात्तिरोदधे ॥
iast:
athendramabruvanmaghavannetadvijānīhi kimetadyakṣamiti tatheti
tadabhyadravattasmāttirodadhe ||
english: Then they said to Indra, 'Maghavan, find out what this wondrous being is.' 'Very well.' He ran towards it, and it vanished from before him.

school_notes.note: Brahman vanished without even speaking to Indra, because his pride in being king of the gods most needed to be broken.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, Indra stays where the being vanished and meets the goddess Uma, whom he asks what it was.
devanagari:
स तस्मिन्नेवाकाशे स्त्रियमाजगाम बहुशोभमानामुमाँ
हैमवतीं ताँहोवाच किमेतद्यक्षमिति ॥
iast:
sa tasminnevākāśe striyamājagāma bahuśobhamānāmumām̐
haimavatīṃ tām̐hovāca kimetadyakṣamiti ||
english: In that very space he came upon a woman of great beauty, Uma, daughter of the Himalaya. He asked her, 'What is this wondrous being?'

school_notes.note: Unlike Agni and Vāyu, Indra did not turn back. Seeing his devotion to the being, knowledge itself appeared in the form of Umā, most beautiful of all; or Umā is the Himalaya's daughter, who is always with the all-knowing Lord and so could answer.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: In the parable, Uma tells Indra the being was Brahman and the victory was Brahman's, and Indra understands.
devanagari:
सा ब्रह्मेति होवाच ब्रह्मणो वा एतद्विजये महीयध्वमिति
ततो हैव विदाञ्चकार ब्रह्मेति ॥
iast:
sā brahmeti hovāca brahmaṇo vā etadvijaye mahīyadhvamiti
tato haiva vidāñcakāra brahmeti ||
english: 'It is Brahman,' she said. 'It was in Brahman's victory that you grew great.' Only then did he know that it was Brahman.

school_notes.note: The demons were defeated by the Lord; the gods were mere instruments, and their 'this victory is ours' was false pride. Indra knew it was Brahman from Umā's words, not by himself.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: The parable concludes that Agni, Vayu and Indra excel the other gods because they came closest to Brahman.
devanagari:
तस्माद्वा एते देवा अतितरामिवान्यान्देवान्यदग्निर्वायुरिन्द्रस्ते
ह्येनन्नेदिष्ठं पस्पर्शुस्ते ह्येनत्प्रथमो विदाञ्चकार ब्रह्मेति ॥
iast:
tasmādvā ete devā atitarāmivānyāndevānyadagnirvāyurindraste
hyenannediṣṭhaṃ pasparśuste hyenatprathamo vidāñcakāra brahmeti ||
english: So these gods, Agni, Vayu and Indra, surpass the other gods, as it were, for they came nearest to it and were the first to know it as Brahman.

school_notes.note: These three excel the others because they came nearest to Brahman, the dearest, by speaking with it or seeing it, and were the foremost to know it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: narrator
context: The parable concludes that Indra excels all the gods because he was the first to know Brahman.
devanagari:
तस्माद्वा इन्द्रोऽतितरामिवान्यान्देवान्
सह्येनन्नेदिष्ठं पस्पर्श स ह्येनत्प्रथमो विदाञ्चकार ब्रह्मेति ॥
iast:
tasmādvā indro'titarāmivānyāndevān
sahyenannediṣṭhaṃ pasparśa sa hyenatprathamo vidāñcakāra brahmeti ||
english: So Indra surpasses the other gods, as it were, for he came nearest to it and was the first to know it as Brahman.

school_notes.note: Agni and Vāyu came to know Brahman through Indra's words, and Indra first heard it from Umā, so Indra excels them all.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Upanishad
context: The Upanishad gives a likeness for Brahman as it touches the world: a flash of lightning, a blink of the eye.
devanagari:
तस्यैष आदेशो यदेतद्विद्युतो व्यद्युतदा३इतीन् न्यमीमिषदा३
इत्यधिदैवतम् ॥
iast:
tasyaiṣa ādeśo yadetadvidyuto vyadyutadā3itīn nyamīmiṣadā3
ityadhidaivatam ||
english: This is the teaching about it, by likeness: as it flashed in the lightning, ah! as it made the eye blink, ah! This is with regard to the divine.

school_notes.note: Since Brahman has no likeness, it is taught by comparison: as lightning flashes once and vanishes, Brahman showed itself to the gods once and vanished; or, like the blink of an eye, it appears and disappears. The prolonged 'ā' marks the comparison.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Upanishad
context: The Upanishad gives a likeness for Brahman within a person: it is what the mind seems to reach when it remembers and resolves.
devanagari:
अथाध्यात्मं यद्देतद्गच्छतीव च मनोऽनेन
चैतदुपस्मरत्यभीक्ष्णँ सङ्कल्पः ॥
iast:
athādhyātmaṃ yaddetadgacchatīva ca mano'nena
caitadupasmaratyabhīkṣṇam̐ saṅkalpaḥ ||
english: Now with regard to the self: the mind seems to go to it, and by the mind one calls it to memory again and again, and resolves upon it.

school_notes.note: Within, Brahman shows itself as if it were an object at the very moment the mind remembers or resolves on it. These likenesses are given because those of slow understanding cannot grasp Brahman free of all conditions.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Upanishad
context: The Upanishad says Brahman is to be meditated on as the one most worth loving, and all beings love one who knows this.
devanagari:
तद्ध तद्वनं नाम तद्वनमित्युपासितव्यं स य एतदेवं वेदाभि
हैनँ सर्वाणि भूतानि संवाञ्छन्ति ॥
iast:
taddha tadvanaṃ nāma tadvanamityupāsitavyaṃ sa ya etadevaṃ vedābhi
hainam̐ sarvāṇi bhūtāni saṃvāñchanti ||
english: It is called Tadvana, 'the one to be loved'; it should be worshipped as Tadvana. All beings long for whoever knows it this way.

school_notes.note: Brahman is 'vana', to be loved and resorted to, being the inner Self of every creature; one who meditates on it under this name is sought after by all beings, as Brahman is.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The student asks for the secret teaching, and the teacher replies that it has already been given.
devanagari:
उपनिषदं भो ब्रूहीत्युक्ता त उपनिषद्ब्राह्मीं वाव त
उपनिषदमब्रूमेति ॥
iast:
upaniṣadaṃ bho brūhītyuktā ta upaniṣadbrāhmīṃ vāva ta
upaniṣadamabrūmeti ||
english: 'Sir, tell me the Upanishad.' 'The Upanishad has been told to you. We have told you the Upanishad about Brahman.'

school_notes.note: The student asks whether the teaching needs some further aid or stands complete. The teacher confirms it is complete; what follows is not an addition to it but the means for gaining it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher names what supports this knowledge: discipline, self-control, work, the Vedas and truthfulness.
devanagari:
तसै तपो दमः कर्मेति प्रतिष्ठा वेदाः सर्वाङ्गानि
सत्यमायतनम् ॥
iast:
tasai tapo damaḥ karmeti pratiṣṭhā vedāḥ sarvāṅgāni
satyamāyatanam ||
english: Austerity, self-control and work are its foundation; the Vedas are all its limbs; truth is its home.

school_notes.note: Austerity and the rest purify the mind so that knowledge arises, in this life or past ones; 'and the like' includes humility and the other virtues of Gita 13.7. Truth means absence of deceit in speech, mind and body; knowledge dwells with the honest, not with the deceitful.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: teacher
context: The teacher closes with the fruit of this knowledge: freedom from evil and a firm place in the infinite.
devanagari:
यो वा एतामेवं वेदापहत्य पाप्मानमनन्ते स्वर्गे
लोके ज्येये प्रतितिष्ठति प्रतितिष्ठति ॥
iast:
yo vā etāmevaṃ vedāpahatya pāpmānamanante svarge
loke jyeye pratitiṣṭhati pratitiṣṭhati ||
english: Whoever knows it in this way strikes away evil and stands firm in the endless, highest heaven, stands firm.

school_notes.note: Whoever knows this knowledge of Brahman shakes off the seed of rebirth, which is ignorance, desire and action, and is established in Brahman, endless and blissful, the supreme Self, never returning to worldly existence.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain
